tldr: Saikali builds a dinner-planning agent step by step in Spring AI, showing that an agent is structured output, tool calling, constraint checks and advisors wired together in plain code.
summary: Saikali (Broadcom) opens with an 'application capability continuum' built around a restaurant booking app: CRUD app, then a machine-learning recommender, then a generative AI Q&A service, and finally an agent that plans the whole dinner. He then argues that ChatGPT and Claude are agents, not models. The ChatGPT app answered a question past its training cutoff by searching the web, where the raw API said it didn't know, and Claude ran `ps aux` in what it said was its own Ubuntu container with Java 21. A model just predicts the next token; tools and a loop make the agent.

With Spring AI's ChatClient he shows system prompts (a 'fruit-only' assistant refusing carrot questions) and structured output. Asking for a Java record makes Spring AI add a JSON schema and formatting instructions to the prompt, which he calls 'prompt begging'. The alternative is the provider's native structured output (opt-in, Spring AI lead Christian Tzolov noted, since not every provider supports it). The first agent module, Jarvis, uses this for intent alignment: each user message is merged into a `UserRequirements` POJO, a plain if-statement lists missing fields, and an enum tracks gathering, confirming and confirmed. When the extracted object `equals()` the previous one, the user has confirmed.

After explaining tool calling with a weather example, he adds a `findAvailableRestaurants` tool over 15 Toronto restaurants. The first search proposes a steakhouse for a vegetarian guest. That leads to his 'iron law': the acceptance rate, meaning the share of tasks users accept without correcting or retrying. The fix is constraint checkers: deterministic ones for budget and noise level returning pass, fail or maybe, an LLM judge for meal suitability, and a hybrid dietary check that sends only main courses to the model. The planner then calls search, detail and check tools and lists only restaurants that pass.

The last modules add decision support, so the agent can compare shortlisted restaurants through a details tool, and Spring AI advisors, which work like servlet filters or AOP around each model call. Tool calling and the model call itself are advisors. A custom advisor plus remember/forget-favourite tools gives the agent user memory. He closes with the two loops: the model decides when to leave the tool-calling loop, while your code decides whether the result meets the constraints. Running the workshop cost about $1.50 on a mini model, and he sees multi-agent orchestration as ordinary service orchestration.
keyPoints: Consumer chat apps are agents with tools (web search, a sandbox VM, memory); the bare API is the closest you get to the raw model, and you bring your own tools.
You can build an agent by writing a SKILL.md, scripting a coding agent such as `claude -p`, or calling the model API directly; the last gives the most control at the highest upfront cost.
Structured output turns free text into Java records: Spring AI either injects a JSON schema into the prompt or uses the provider's native response format, which is opt-in.
Intent alignment keeps requirements in a typed object; missing-field checks are plain if-statements, and an unchanged object after a user message is read as confirmation.

Tool calling is the model answering with a request to call a method; Spring AI invokes `@Tool`-annotated methods, sends back the result and repeats, and the model decides how many calls to make, for example one weather call per city.
MCP is presented as tool calling run out of process, so tools can be written in any language and shared across host applications.

Constraint checkers come in three kinds: deterministic (budget range, noise level), LLM judge (meal suitability, returning a record with verdict and reason), and hybrid (filter the menu to main courses, then ask the model about dietary fit).
Spring AI advisors form a filter chain around each model call; tool calling, observability and the model call itself are advisors, and a custom advisor can add memory such as favourite restaurants.
takeaways: Measure your agent by acceptance rate, meaning tasks users accept without correction, and collect token, latency and cost metrics from day one.
Capture user intent in a typed object with structured output before letting the agent act, and check for missing fields in plain code.
Write verifiable checks for every hard constraint, deterministic where possible and narrowly scoped LLM judges where not, and only show results that pass.
Give each model call its own focused system prompt, and use a cheap model for extraction and a stronger one for planning.
Use an advisor (or your framework's interceptor) for cross-cutting concerns such as memory, tracing and guardrails instead of repeating them at every call site.

quotes.text: The consumer apps are agents. They're not models.
Acceptance is a system property. It's not the model's fault. It's not your agent's fault. It's both.
Who decides to exit the tool calling loop? The model does, not your code.

watchIf: You are a Java developer who uses chat assistants but has never built an agent, and want a clear mental model of what happens on the wire.
